items.summary_html:
Welcome back to the React Mastery Series!

In the previous article, we explored Custom Hooks in React and learned how reusable logic helps developers build scalable and maintainable applications.

Today, we will explore one of the most important concepts in modern frontend development:

React Routing

Almost every real-world React application contains multiple screens:

  • Login
  • Dashboard
  • Profile
  • Settings
  • Reports
  • Transactions
  • Admin panels

But React applications are usually built as:

Single Page Applications (SPA)

So how do we navigate between different pages without refreshing the browser?

The answer is React Router

What is Client-Side Routing?

Traditional websites work like this:

User Clicks Link
       |
       ↓
Browser Requests New HTML Page
       |
       ↓
Server Sends Page
       |
       ↓
Browser Reloads

Every navigation causes a full page refresh.

React Single Page Applications work differently:

User Clicks Link
       |
       ↓
React Router Intercepts Request
       |
       ↓
URL Changes
       |
       ↓
React Loads Component
       |
       ↓
No Page Refresh

This creates a smooth application experience.

What is React Router?

React Router is a library that enables navigation between different components based on the URL.

Example:

/login
/dashboard
/profile
/settings

Each URL maps to a React component.

Example:

/login
   |
   ↓
Login Component


/dashboard
   |
   ↓
Dashboard Component
Installing React Router

For a React application:

npm install react-router-dom

The package provides:

  • BrowserRouter
  • Routes
  • Route
  • Link
  • Navigate
  • useNavigate
  • useParams
Setting Up BrowserRouter

The first step is wrapping your application.

Example:

import { BrowserRouter } from "react-router-dom";

import App from "./App";

ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById("root")).render(
  <BrowserRouter>
    <App />
  BrowserRouter>,
);

Now React can manage browser navigation.

Creating Routes

Routes define which component should display for a URL.

Example:

import { Routes, Route } from "react-router-dom";

function App() {
  return (
    <Routes>
      <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />

      <Route path="/login" element={<Login />} />

      <Route path="/dashboard" element={<Dashboard />} />
    Routes>
  );
}

Now:

/login

renders:

<Login />
Understanding Route Components

Example:

<Route path="/profile" element={<Profile />} />;

Contains path and element

The URL path specifies the url appeared in browser

Example:

/profile
element

The component to render on visiting the path specified.

Example:

<Profile />
Navigation Using Link

Traditional HTML - causes a browser refresh.

 href="/dashboard"> Dashboard

React Router provides:

import { Link } from "react-router-dom";
<Link to="/dashboard">DashboardLink>

Benefits:

  • No page refresh
  • SPA behavior
  • Better performance
Creating a Navigation Bar

Example:

function Navbar() {
  return (
    <nav>
      <Link to="/">HomeLink>

      <Link to="/dashboard">DashboardLink>

      <Link to="/profile">ProfileLink>
    nav>
  );
}

When users click:

Dashboard

React loads:

<Dashboard />

without refreshing.

Programmatic Navigation with useNavigate

Sometimes navigation happens after an action.

Examples:

  • Successful login
  • Logout
  • Form submission

Example:

import { useNavigate } from "react-router-dom";

function Login() {
  const navigate = useNavigate();

  function handleLogin() {
    // API success

    navigate("/dashboard");
  }

  return <button onClick={handleLogin}>Loginbutton>;
}

Flow:

User Login
     |
     ↓
API Success
     |
     ↓
navigate("/dashboard")
     |
     ↓
Dashboard Page
Route Parameters

Many applications need dynamic URLs.

Example:

/users/101

Here:

101

is dynamic.

React Router supports this using parameters.

Example:

<Route path="/users/:id" element={<UserDetails />} />
Reading Route Parameters

Using:

useParams()

Example:

import { useParams } from "react-router-dom";

function UserDetails() {
  const { id } = useParams();

  return <h2>User ID: {id}h2>;
}

URL:

/users/101

Output:

User ID: 101
Real-World Example: Banking Application

Consider:

/accounts/12345

where:

12345

is the account number.

Route:

<Route path="/accounts/:accountId" element={<AccountDetails />} />

Component:

const { accountId }=useParams();

Now the application knows which account to display.

Nested Routes

Large applications often have sections inside sections.

Example:

Dashboard

   |
   ├── Overview

   ├── Transactions

   └── Profile

Routes:

<Route>
  <Route path="/dashboard" element={<Dashboard />} >
  <Route path="transactions" element={<Transactions />} />
  <Route path="profile" element={<Profile />} />
Routes>

URL:

/dashboard/transactions

renders:

Dashboard
    +
Transactions
Outlet Component

Nested routes use:

<Outlet />

Example:

import { Outlet } from "react-router-dom";

function Dashboard() {
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Dashboardh1>

      <Outlet />
    div>
  );
}

The child route appears where Outlet exists.

Protected Routes

Enterprise applications often require authentication.

Example:

Users should access:

/dashboard

only after login.

Without authentication:

/dashboard
       |
       ↓
Redirect
       |
       ↓
/login
Creating ProtectedRoute

Example:

function ProtectedRoute({ children }) {
  const isAuthenticated = true;

  if (!isAuthenticated) {
    return <Navigate to="/login" />;
  }

  return children;
}

Usage:

<Route
  path="/dashboard"

  element={
    <ProtectedRoute>
      <Dashboard />
    ProtectedRoute>
  }
/>;
Real-World Authentication Flow

Enterprise applications usually follow:

User Opens Application

        |
        ↓

Check Token

        |
        ↓

Token Exists?

        |
   -------------
   |           |
 Yes           No
   |            |
Dashboard     Login

React Router handles navigation decisions.

Lazy Loading Routes

Large applications should not load every page immediately.

Example:

const Dashboard = lazy(() => import("./Dashboard") );

Route:

<Suspense fallback="Loading...">
  <Routes>
    <Route path="/dashboard" element={<Dashboard />} />
  Routes>
Suspense>;

Benefits:

  • Smaller initial bundle
  • Faster startup
  • Better performance
Route Organization in Enterprise Projects

A scalable structure:

src

├── routes
│    ├── AppRoutes.jsx
│    ├── ProtectedRoute.jsx
├── pages
│    ├── Login.jsx
│    ├── Dashboard.jsx
│    └── Profile.jsx
├── layouts
│    └── MainLayout.jsx
Real-World Banking Application Routing

Example:

/login

/dashboard

/accounts

/accounts/:id

/transactions

/profile

/settings

Flow:

Login
 |
 ↓
Authentication Success
 |
 ↓
Dashboard
 |
 ├── Accounts
 |
 ├── Transactions
 |
 └── Profile

This is the architecture used in many enterprise React applications.

Common Mistakes 1. Using Anchor Tags

Avoid:

 href="/dashboard"> Dashboard

Use:

<Link to="/dashboard"> Dashboard Link>
2. Forgetting BrowserRouter

Without:

<BrowserRouter>

routing will not work.

3. Incorrect Nested Routes

Parent route must contain:

<Outlet />

otherwise child routes won't appear.

4. Loading All Pages at Startup

Large applications should use:

  • lazy loading
  • code splitting
Best Practices
  • Keep routes centralized.
  • Use lazy loading for large applications.
  • Create reusable protected routes.
  • Use meaningful URL structures.
  • Avoid unnecessary route nesting.
  • Separate page components from reusable components.
Key Takeaways

Today, we learned:

✅ React Router enables navigation in Single Page Applications.
✅ Routes map URLs to React components.
✅ Link provides SPA navigation without refresh.
✅ useNavigate enables programmatic navigation.
✅ useParams reads dynamic route values.
✅ Protected routes secure application pages.
✅ Lazy loading improves application performance.

Coming Next 🚀

In Day 20, we will explore:

Building Production-Ready React Applications – Project Structure and Architecture

We will learn:

  • Scalable folder structure
  • Component organization
  • Feature-based architecture
  • Separation of concerns
  • API service layers
  • Error handling
  • Environment configuration
  • Enterprise React project patterns

This will connect all the concepts we learned so far into a real-world production architecture.

Happy Coding! 🚀

items.title: Read the cold LinkedIn outreach that led Fishwife's CEO to hire a candidate
items.summary: Becca Millstein said this one LinkedIn message stood out. Fishwife Becca Millstein, cofounder and CEO of Fishwife, said she doesn't typically respond to DMs. However, she recently hired a candidate after they sent an effective LinkedIn outreach. She said the candidate had a great background, strong numbers to back it up, and a concise message. If you feel like your messages are getting lost in the void, you may be onto something. Executives are often bombarded with many sales pitches and introductions every day — and that makes it difficult to stand out with a cold outreach . Becca Millstein, cofounder and CEO of the trendy tinned seafood company Fishwife, said she misses many of the messages she receives on LinkedIn. "I don't respond to DMs because I don't see them, or it's just too much," Millstein told Business Insider. Millstein, who cofounded the company in 2020, said it's become increasingly difficult for candidates to stand out by sending a direct message. Every so often, though, someone manages to break through. She said a prospective employee reached out several months ago. After seeing the message, she passed it on to the hiring manager, and they ultimately hired the candidate. An anonymized version of the DM is below: Hi Becca, I just applied for the ______ role at Fishwife and wanted to introduce myself. In ______ years at ______, I've scaled ______  from ______ to ______ M orders/year. I oversee end-to-end ______, including ______, while managing the corresponding budget of $______ M/year. In addition to leading ______, I'm responsible for our relationships and agreements with ______. I use data to forecast ______, and to optimize______. The best part of my role is the cross-functional collaboration with teams like ______. Would you be open to a conversation to discuss the role further? My résumé is attached for reference. Thanks! Millstein said the candidate's message got her attention because it was specific and direct. They explained which role they were interested in, summarized their relevant experience, and included numbers to make their case. She added that the message was concise and made it clear they were "clearly not a robot," which stands out in the flood of messages she receives. The CEO said that after checking the candidate out, she sent the résumé to the hiring manager and said, "This person seems awesome." Most of the messages she receives "don't have that kind of substance," Millstein said. The candidate also included their résumé in the message and said they had already applied for the job, which Millstein said was an important detail. "Never just send a message if there's a job application open," Millstein said. "Apply for that job. You'll get lost if you don't." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Your agent's memory is a vector store. Ask it "how many" and watch it fall over.
items.summary: Originally published at nlqdb.com/blog The standard agent-memory build is an afternoon of work: embed every fact worth keeping, upsert it into a vector store, and before each reply pull the top-k most similar memories back into context. And for what it's built for, it works. Ask "what did this user say about the Berlin migration" and the right snippets come back, ranked by cosine distance. Recall is solved enough that it feels like memory is solved. Then the agent has been running for a month, and you ask its memory a different kind of question: "how many users asked about pricing this month?" "Average deal size per stage?" "Top 10 topics I logged, ranked by count?" The store dutifully returns the twenty memories most similar to the question text , the LLM eyeballs them, and you get a confident, specific, wrong number. Recall is similarity. Reporting is aggregation. Nothing malfunctioned — the two questions want different machines. A vector store's primitive is nearest-neighbour search: embed the query, rank stored vectors by distance, return the top-k, optionally narrowed by a metadata filter. That is the whole contract. There is no COUNT , no GROUP BY , no JOIN , no HAVING — a similarity engine ships no query planner, and even the metadata filter only narrows candidates around the approximate search, so what comes back is still a ranking of similar items, never a computed result set. "How many" has to touch every matching row . If the agent logged 4,000 memories and top-k is 20, the context the LLM sees is structurally incapable of producing the count — and an LLM doing arithmetic over a retrieved sample is a hallucination generator, not a query engine. The failure is quiet, too: the answer arrives fluent and plausible, and nothing flags that it was computed from half a percent of the data. -- "top topics this month, ranked by count" is not a similarity query. -- It's this — and it must scan every matching row, not the top-k: SELECT topic , count ( * ) AS mentions FROM memories WHERE created_at >= date_trunc ( 'month' , now ()) GROUP BY topic ORDER BY mentions DESC LIMIT 10 ; So the split worth keeping: when the question is "find what's like this" — RAG context, related-document lookup, fuzzy recall over conversation — a vector store is exactly the right machine, and a managed one like Pinecone is genuinely good at it. When the question is "count, group, or rank what I stored" , the memory needs to be typed rows behind a real query planner. Neither machine substitutes for the other, and bolting a bigger LLM onto the first one doesn't turn it into the second. They compose cleanly: vector store as the recall layer, relational store as the analytical one. That second layer is what nlqdb is — a real Postgres the agent provisions itself over MCP and queries in plain English, with the compiled SQL shown so you can read exactly what ran. The honest caveat cuts the other way too: nlqdb ships no embedding search, so it is not your recall layer. Pick the store per question shape — the full side-by-side is at nlqdb vs Pinecone .

items.title: He turned a side hustle into a video game resale business that's brought in $4 million this year
items.summary: Caleb Ashton is the owner and founder of QuickFlips. QuickFlips Caleb Ashton founded QuickFlips, a platform to sell video games, consoles, and Pokémon cards. Ashton opened a storefront for his business in 2025. QuickFlips has paid customers over $5 million since 2019. Caleb Ashton's journey into the resale business was, like many who start out in that industry, humble. Ashton began flipping items — textbooks, action figures, golf clubs, sneakers, and more — while living with his wife in a one-bedroom apartment in 2019. He was eager to create an extra source of income while his wife attended law school. In true millennial fashion, he learned how to buy and resell items from YouTube videos. "I started with a budget of 500 bucks that I had cobbled together from birthday and Christmas money. That was my startup seed money," Ashton, 31, told Business Insider."I initially focused on really cheap items like books or things that I could get for $5 at yard sales." Caleb Ashton opened a storefront for his business, QuickFlips, in Kentucky. QuickFlips Ashton kept up the side hustle for about six months, but it turned into a full-time job after he was fired from a friend's collectible coin business. By that point, Ashton had learned that some items could lead to quick, reliable money. Specifically, physical video games. Things grew quickly. In 2024, he created QuickFlips , an online resale platform where people can sell their video game collections, consoles, and Pokémon trading cards . He also built the platform's buyback software system. On QuickFlips, users enter their item into the search bar to get an instant offer price. Once the QuickFlips team has inspected the incoming items, users ship them to the company and receive a payout within 24 hours. QuickFlips then resells the refurbished items on Amazon, eBay, and TCGPlayer to make a profit. As of 2025, they're also sold in Ashton's brick-and-mortar store. Users can find payout prices for different items through QuickFlips' search bar. QuickFlips Ashton opened the storefront last September in Lexington, Kentucky. The overall business made about $4 million in revenue in 2026 and has paid over $5 million to customers since its inception. Necessity becomes invention Ashton's decision to open a storefront came out of necessity. For a time, he operated QuickFlips from his spare bedroom. Then, his basement. "My first hire was my friend Spencer, who came to help pack stuff up and list inventory," Ashton said. "We ended up having about 10 employees in that basement." QuickFlips began purchasing dozens of video game collections each week. That meant storing the numerous collections, assessing the products, listing them for sale on sites like Amazon , and preparing them for shipping, all from the basement. At one point, there was so much inventory in the basement that Ashton struggled to find space for new hires. "It was way too tight. My neighbors hated me, so I knew I had to get an actual office space. We landed on a retail complex," Ashton said. QuickFlips now has 33 employees across its storefront and online platform. QuickFlips Now, QuickFlips has 33 employees across its online platform and retail space. Strategy-wide, Ashton said QuickFlip's approach to payouts is what differentiates it from other sellers in the marketplace. They have a simple motto: "Pay well, Sell fast." "We offer a transparent offer upfront. We don't say, 'Hey, come to our store, and we'll make you an offer after we look at everything,'" Ashton said. "We say, 'As long as this is in good condition, we will give you this much for it.'" Ashton said his business is focused on moving volume. "We're not necessarily focused on getting every penny for every item," Ashton said. "We would prefer to get some of the money all the time, rather than all the money some of the time." Going analog Selling physical video games and consoles may sound like a dead end in the AI age, but Ashton has learned otherwise. Nostalgia is a tried-and-true driver of sales. "A big reason that people collect, in general, is to go back to a simpler time. There's significant value for a lot of folks," Ashton said. "Another thing is that a lot of folks we've found are getting fed up with digital media." The influx of digital media and products these days has led some consumers to seek out physical alternatives . Manufacturers and thrift shop owners have told Business Insider they've noticed items like the Nintendo DS become popular with younger generations. Physical media sold at stores like QuickFlips has become popular with younger generations. QuickFlips In the gaming community, Sony inadvertently sparked calls for more physical games when it announced that production of PlayStation discs for new games would end in 2028. "Every day, servers are getting shut down. Games are becoming inaccessible. People are realizing that we don't actually own these digital games," Ashton said. "Sometimes people will come in to trade their PS5 that has 50 games on it, and be crushed when they realize that doesn't actually give the console any more value because we're going to have to reset it." Living in a world with social media does have some perks, though. QuickFlips has amassed over 661,000 subscribers across its accounts, which also earn ad revenue. "There are very few people in the space that have our social media following," Ashton said. "There are hundreds of thousands of collectors and video game resellers that know who we are because of how much we invest into our YouTube, Instagram, and Facebook content." Ashton chronicles QuickFlips growth and his experience as an entrepreneur on his YouTube page, Phoenix Resale . It's our goal to provide a lot of value to people upfront on both the education and entertainment side," Ashton said. "That's a big part of why they choose to do business with us." "It was way too tight. My neighbors hated me, so I knew I had to get an actual office space. We landed on a retail complex," Ashton said.

QuickFlips now has 33 employees across its storefront and online platform.

QuickFlips

Now, QuickFlips has 33 employees across its online platform and retail space. Strategy-wide, Ashton said QuickFlip's approach to payouts is what differentiates it from other sellers in the marketplace. They have a simple motto: "Pay well, Sell fast."

"We offer a transparent offer upfront. We don't say, 'Hey, come to our store, and we'll make you an offer after we look at everything,'" Ashton said. "We say, 'As long as this is in good condition, we will give you this much for it.'"

Ashton said his business is focused on moving volume.

"We're not necessarily focused on getting every penny for every item," Ashton said. "We would prefer to get some of the money all the time, rather than all the money some of the time."

Going analog

Selling physical video games and consoles may sound like a dead end in the AI age, but Ashton has learned otherwise. Nostalgia is a tried-and-true driver of sales.

"A big reason that people collect, in general, is to go back to a simpler time. There's significant value for a lot of folks," Ashton said. "Another thing is that a lot of folks we've found are getting fed up with digital media."

The influx of digital media and products these days has led some consumers to seek out physical alternatives. Manufacturers and thrift shop owners have told Business Insider they've noticed items like the Nintendo DS become popular with younger generations.

Physical media sold at stores like QuickFlips has become popular with younger generations.

QuickFlips

In the gaming community, Sony inadvertently sparked calls for more physical games when it announced that production of PlayStation discs for new games would end in 2028.

"Every day, servers are getting shut down. Games are becoming inaccessible. People are realizing that we don't actually own these digital games," Ashton said. "Sometimes people will come in to trade their PS5 that has 50 games on it, and be crushed when they realize that doesn't actually give the console any more value because we're going to have to reset it."

Living in a world with social media does have some perks, though. QuickFlips has amassed over 661,000 subscribers across its accounts, which also earn ad revenue.

"There are very few people in the space that have our social media following," Ashton said. "There are hundreds of thousands of collectors and video game resellers that know who we are because of how much we invest into our YouTube, Instagram, and Facebook content."

Ashton chronicles QuickFlips growth and his experience as an entrepreneur on his YouTube page, Phoenix Resale.

It's our goal to provide a lot of value to people upfront on both the education and entertainment side," Ashton said. "That's a big part of why they choose to do business with us."

items.title: DoorDash is paying people to load its delivery robots. It points to a shortcoming of automation
items.summary: DoorDash is paying gig workers to load restaurant orders into its Dot robots. Bloomberg/Getty Images DoorDash's Dot delivery robot can't physically pick up restaurant orders on its own. The company is paying gig workers to cover the final feet between restaurants and the robots. DoorDash said that it's offering the loading gigs to meet demand during busy times. DoorDash's delivery robots need a hand. Some workers in areas where DoorDash is using its Dot delivery robot are receiving offers through the DoorDash app to load them up. While the vehicles can navigate miles to delivery destinations, it's the few feet between a restaurant's pickup counter and the curb outside where delivery workers intervene. Devena Bybee, a DoorDash gig worker in Mesa, Arizona, said that she received one such offer in early July. The company is using the robots to make deliveries in the Phoenix area. Bybee drove about two miles to a restaurant, picked up an order, and placed it in the Dot robot as it waited in the parking lot, she said. She took photos of each step to document the process, and the gig took five minutes, she said. DoorDash paid her about $5. Bybee was surprised that Doordash asked her to complete the task instead of a restaurant worker who was already on-site. "I just don't see how it's efficient," she said. On Facebook groups for DoorDash workers, some posts show screenshots of similar gig offers over the past month. "I would never do a five-dollar order, but I was really curious about this and I was super close to the restaurant," reads one July 6 post showing a robot-loading gig at a Burger King in Scottsdale, Arizona. The poster did not immediately respond to a request for comment. "Dashers are essential to our platform and will continue completing the majority of deliveries even as our autonomous technology scales," a DoorDash spokesperson said. "This limited pilot is designed to support merchants during busy periods, while creating more earning opportunities for Dashers outside of traditional deliveries," the spokesperson added. A sticking point for automation The loading gigs are the latest example of DoorDash workers stepping in when autonomous vehicles can't complete a job on their own. Some workers received offers from DoorDash to close open doors on Waymo's self-driving cars in Atlanta, Business Insider reported in February. Waymo plans to add a self-closing function to its vehicles in the future, the companies said at the time. Dot, which DoorDash unveiled in September, is roughly the size of a baby stroller and can hold up to 30 pounds of cargo. The robot can navigate both roads and sidewalks to travel between restaurants and customers' homes. Handing off orders from restaurants to robots is a challenge to the rollout of autonomous deliveries , DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said last August, shortly before the company debuted Dot. While loading an order only takes a few minutes, restaurants that receive lots of robot-delivered orders might have an incentive to outsource the task to DoorDash, said Robert Bruno, a professor of labor and employment relations at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. DoorDash's gig workers, who are independent contractors, don't receive the same employee benefits and hourly pay rate that most restaurant workers do, Bruno said. "Multiplied over the course of a year or more, there's probably a real savings," he said. Bybee, the DoorDash worker in Arizona, said that the loading gig left her more confident that humans are still needed for delivery work. "There's only so much right now that the robots can do," she said. Do you have a story idea about DoorDash? items.title: I sold my house in Miami and moved to rural North Florida. My cost of living and stress are down, and productivity is up.
items.summary: Cheryl Patella. Courtesy of Cheryl Patella Cheryl Patella transformed her life by moving from Miami to rural North Florida. Her move cut her commuting costs, improved her quality of life, and aligned her work with personal values. Embracing remote work, Patella now enjoys nature, reduced expenses, and intentional living in Florida. At 6 a.m. every morning, I gather fresh eggs, check the vegetable garden, breathe in the cool North Florida air, watch my dogs race across five acres, and walk into my home office to begin a virtual meeting with a client. Five years ago, my mornings began very differently. Before sunrise, I had already left my home in Miami and was in bumper-to-bumper traffic on Interstate 95. My commute to my job, which began as a fitness director and advanced to acting spa director and later as spa director at another facility, had stretched from 35 to 50 minutes, plus a 20-minute ferry ride. I paid about $65 a week in tolls, drove 20,000 to 22,000 miles each year, and accepted nearly two hours of commuting as simply part of building a successful career. I believed those sacrifices were the cost of doing business Our culture often presents a choice between pursuing success and living a simpler life. What I didn't recognize was that I was also paying hidden quality-of-life costs in time, attention, stress, and mental energy, which diminished both the quantity and quality of my work. They never appeared on a budget, yet they quietly influenced how I lived, worked, and thought. Ironically, after more than four decades helping clients improve their physical and emotional well-being as a medical fitness specialist, I hadn't fully recognized how much my own environment was shaping mine. Then COVID-19 created something unexpected For the first time in decades, life became quiet enough for me to step back and evaluate the life I had built. I suddenly found myself with enough distance from my normal routine to ask questions I had been too busy to consider before. I started looking for a vacation home where I could spend more time outdoors with my dogs. Then someone asked what my dream home would look like if I could live anywhere. I wrote it down, and the search quietly shifted toward finding a new place to live full-time. I kept picturing myself sitting at a desk in a wooded area, writing. The vision came to life while searching on Zillow and yielded three top choices. It was quite an experience searching for homes in the mountains Some were too far from anyone I knew, and others would have a serious winter season, which was foreign to me. I flew to each of those cities and, after inspecting several properties, I made a list of the pros and cons of each. It came down to a North Florida property. It was closer to family and a bit larger than I had in mind, but it had all the specifics I was looking for: woods, land, seasonal changes, and they accepted a lower offer. As a Christian, I've always made prayer part of my decision-making. Over time, I became convinced God wasn't asking me to escape my life — he was asking me to realign it. The decision also made practical sense Real estate in South Florida had skyrocketed, and my home in Miami had appreciated substantially. Selling it allowed me to buy 5.5 acres at 59% of my Miami home's selling price, left me with the funds needed for remodeling and upgrades, and reduced recurring expenses. I moved some of my clients to a new trainer who was a good fit for them. Two clients wished to remain with me and work remotely. The home I bought was a foreclosure, which meant it could take three months or more to close, requiring me to stay in a rental or hotel with my dogs — another serious adjustment. Finally spending almost two years remodeling the house tested my patience more than I expected. Like any worthwhile investment, the return has unfolded over time. My property has appreciated to double the price I paid for it. Nearly five years later, I can say it was worth every challenge Patella with her dogs on her porch. Courtesy of Cheryl Patella In South Florida, I spent weekends on my Jet Ski . Flying across Biscayne Bay felt like the perfect escape from a demanding workweek. Occasionally, dolphins would surface nearby, jumping alongside me as I crossed the water. I've traded my Jet Ski for a Hustler zero-turn lawn mower. I spend time maintaining pastures, tending gardens, and caring for the property that has become my sanctuary. The wildlife encounters haven't disappeared — they've simply changed. I now watch small herds of deer graze peacefully in the fields. Some of the financial benefits were obvious. My auto insurance premium dropped from $280 to about $125 a month after moving north. Homeowners insurance fell from roughly $4,000 a year to $1,800, and property taxes declined from $4,000 annually to $1,600. My monthly fuel bill was cut by more than half, tolls virtually disappeared, and my current vehicle, purchased new in 2023, has under 20,000 miles after nearly three years. My work has changed as well Technology allows me to work with clients across the country, but the biggest change wasn't where I work — it was how I work. For years, I managed teams of 30 to 40 employees while supporting communities of several thousand elite residents. It was fulfilling, but every day required constant decisions, interruptions, staffing issues, and operational problem-solving. Today, my office overlooks gardens, open fields, and woods. When I need a break, I step outside and walk the property, work in the garden, or watch deer cross the pasture before returning to my desk. Other changes happened because my environment changed Living in Miami made it easy to stop for lunch, meet friends for dinner, shop on the way home, or spend money simply because everything was convenient. I'd always encouraged my clients to prepare meals in advance because it saves time, reduces impulse eating, and lowers food costs. Living in a rural community makes it easier to consistently practice those habits. Restaurants are no longer around every corner, and shopping has become intentional rather than convenient. Weekly dry cleaning, salon appointments, dog-walking services, and a home alarm system disappeared. Professional suits and designer shoes gradually gave way to jeans, work boots, and workout clothes. Acreage, however, requires equipment, fencing, landscaping, and continual upkeep that doesn't exist on a suburban lot. Travel is less convenient, too. Instead of flying directly from Miami to almost anywhere, most trips now require connections. There are other trade-offs I miss having my niece and her children nearby, but we talk almost daily, and we've traveled together around the US and to Europe. I also miss my longtime housekeeper, who knew my home, my routines, and my dogs almost as well as I did. Every meaningful decision asks us to give something up Somewhere along the way, I became so immersed in the business of doing business that I stopped evaluating my quality of life. Living in the country doesn't equate with loneliness, as my days are still filled with Zooms and FaceTimes. I have close neighbors who watch out for me, and when I need something, I call them. The difference is that I traded constant interruption for intentional connection. My cost of living declined, my productivity increased, my stress level fell, and my quality of life has improved, but the greatest return wasn't measured by lower insurance premiums, fewer tolls, or a shorter commute. It came from finally aligning my faith, my values, my work, and the life I wanted to build. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: At an ex-OpenAI researcher's influential lab, $500,000 salaries aren't enough to fix a talent 'bottleneck'
items.summary: METR's CEO, Beth Barnes, and president, Chris Painter. METR METR, a Berkeley lab started by an ex-OpenAI researcher, has grown into a prominent AI umpire. The nonprofit works with OpenAI, Anthropic, and governments to evaluate cutting-edge models. METR says that an AI talent shortage hinders growth in safety and security research. Beth Barnes, one of the AI industry's most influential watchdogs, has a lot to worry about. The ex-OpenAI researcher has shown that AI's capabilities are escalating by the month . Now, she fears that the industry doesn't have the staff in place to keep up with the technology in its next chapter. The biggest barrier to that research is talent, said Barnes, who left OpenAI to start the nonprofit METR in 2022. METR, which stands for Model Evaluation and Threat Research, plays a crucial role in the AI industry by working closely with OpenAI, Anthropic , Google, and Meta to provide independent answers about the tech's quickly changing capabilities. Yet Barnes sees such fierce competition for AI researchers that even METR's lofty salaries, which reach $503,000 on current job postings, don't address the nonprofit's talent shortage. "Ideally, we'd like to scale really large, but in practice, we've been able to fundraise as much as we need, and the bottleneck is much more talent," Barnes said. The security incident announced by OpenAI and Hugging Face sparked a new wave of questions about how to evaluate and control AI. More than 1,300 frontier lab employees signed a letter in July warning that AI development could outpace control. If the industry doesn't have the staff to research precisely what new AI models can do, companies could be forced to slow their releases. While the behavior of the OpenAI models stunned much of the corporate world, METR's team was far less surprised. Governments, companies, and even religious groups all ask the nonprofit for help understanding and testing the tech's progress. Still, the feeling inside the 35-person lab is one of concern. When Business Insider visited METR's Berkeley office on the afternoon that OpenAI revealed its hack, Barnes described an AI safety field that is badly constrained by its size. "There's so much more to do than we have capacity for," Barnes said. A "reasonable civilization," in her view, would be pouring a far larger percentage of AI's investment into steering it and evaluating the tech — especially now that society is reckoning with models this powerful. 'Humanity's preparedness team' struggles to grow As AI labs release new models, METR measures the likelihood that they can complete tasks of increasing duration. These measurements form the nonprofit's most famous offering, a widely-cited chart that shows how, over the last six years, AI's capabilities have doubled about every seven months. Chris Painter, METR's president, describes the lab as "humanity's preparedness team," a tongue-in-cheek nod to the preparedness teams at OpenAI and Anthropic that report safety threats to their CEOs. "We aren't really accountable to anyone other than the public and the public's well-being," Painter said. METR employees work at their office in Berkeley. Stephen Council/Business Insider Barnes emphasized the importance of METR's independence so that it can produce research that isn't tied to a company's goals. When Barnes worked at OpenAI, she felt the need for a research group outside the labs that could comment freely on the development of the tech. While METR doesn't take money from the frontier AI labs or their employees, it accepts compute grants and works with them to analyze unreleased models. In addition, staff have analyzed labs' safety practices, written about AI's effect on software engineers' speed, and studied the merits of using AI models to monitor other AI models. Barnes said she'd like to expand into predicting the next levels of AI's capabilities and how those changes could accelerate AI's development. Neev Parikh, a METR researcher, says talent constraints limit the number of questions researchers can tackle about AI models' internal reasoning. "There's a dearth of people," Parikh said. "I would happily see the field expand 10x." METR could play a big role in a new AI climate In July, OpenAI announced that its AI models cheated during testing by hacking into Hugging Face's systems to find the test answers. Later, CEO Sam Altman said it was "the first security incident that I have felt very viscerally." METR had seen something like that coming. In May, the nonprofit wrote in a report that current AI agents "could plausibly start a rogue deployment," but would not have the skill to hide it. Then, in June, METR tried out OpenAI's then-unreleased GPT-5.6 Sol model and found that it would repeatedly cheat on challenging tests, including by extracting hidden source code to find the answers. It published a report about this and shared it with OpenAI before GPT-5.6 Sol's wider release . Come July, the GPT-5.6 Sol model was part of OpenAI's security incident with Hugging Face . OpenAI announced on Wednesday that METR and another nonprofit, Redwood Research, would assess the incident and that their results would inform OpenAI's own technical report. "There are now real, business-affecting incidents of this, and the world has a stake in understanding that," Painter said. The cyber skills of OpenAI and Anthropic's newest models have sparked a wave of fear and attention and spawned a raft of new bills in Washington . METR's work lines up closely with one potential route for regulation: a current bill proposal would require large AI model developers to get safety audits from outside organizations. METR could fill a role like this; Painter said they'd potentially be interested, though it's something the field is still figuring out. Something like that proposal, Painter said, could help with METR's hiring issue. He suggested that more people might leave the AI companies themselves — for similar salaries at METR, though without equity compensation — if a regulatory system gave safety research organizations greater authority. "There's enough precedent here for each kind of testing arrangement," Painter said, "that I think with either clarity from industry, about how this testing should work long-term, or from the government, I think this field could scale very rapidly." Ajeya Cotra, who led the writing of METR's May report on the risks of AI, said that oversight of AI can feel "chaotic and unpredictable" right now. She's still optimistic. "The trend is toward people caring about this issue more," Cotra said. "And wanting to regulate it in a more serious way over time." Have a tip?   • The nonprofit works with OpenAI, Anthropic, and governments to evaluate cutting-edge models.
  • METR says that an AI talent shortage hinders growth in safety and security research.

Beth Barnes, one of the AI industry's most influential watchdogs, has a lot to worry about.

The ex-OpenAI researcher has shown that AI's capabilities are escalating by the month. Now, she fears that the industry doesn't have the staff in place to keep up with the technology in its next chapter.

The biggest barrier to that research is talent, said Barnes, who left OpenAI to start the nonprofit METR in 2022. METR, which stands for Model Evaluation and Threat Research, plays a crucial role in the AI industry by working closely with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta to provide independent answers about the tech's quickly changing capabilities.

Yet Barnes sees such fierce competition for AI researchers that even METR's lofty salaries, which reach $503,000 on current job postings, don't address the nonprofit's talent shortage.

"Ideally, we'd like to scale really large, but in practice, we've been able to fundraise as much as we need, and the bottleneck is much more talent," Barnes said.

The security incident announced by OpenAI and Hugging Face sparked a new wave of questions about how to evaluate and control AI. More than 1,300 frontier lab employees signed a letter in July warning that AI development could outpace control. If the industry doesn't have the staff to research precisely what new AI models can do, companies could be forced to slow their releases.

While the behavior of the OpenAI models stunned much of the corporate world, METR's team was far less surprised. Governments, companies, and even religious groups all ask the nonprofit for help understanding and testing the tech's progress.

Still, the feeling inside the 35-person lab is one of concern. When Business Insider visited METR's Berkeley office on the afternoon that OpenAI revealed its hack, Barnes described an AI safety field that is badly constrained by its size.

"There's so much more to do than we have capacity for," Barnes said. A "reasonable civilization," in her view, would be pouring a far larger percentage of AI's investment into steering it and evaluating the tech — especially now that society is reckoning with models this powerful.

'Humanity's preparedness team' struggles to grow

As AI labs release new models, METR measures the likelihood that they can complete tasks of increasing duration. These measurements form the nonprofit's most famous offering, a widely-cited chart that shows how, over the last six years, AI's capabilities have doubled about every seven months.

Chris Painter, METR's president, describes the lab as "humanity's preparedness team," a tongue-in-cheek nod to the preparedness teams at OpenAI and Anthropic that report safety threats to their CEOs.

"We aren't really accountable to anyone other than the public and the public's well-being," Painter said.

METR employees work at their office in Berkeley.

Stephen Council/Business Insider

Barnes emphasized the importance of METR's independence so that it can produce research that isn't tied to a company's goals. When Barnes worked at OpenAI, she felt the need for a research group outside the labs that could comment freely on the development of the tech. While METR doesn't take money from the frontier AI labs or their employees, it accepts compute grants and works with them to analyze unreleased models.

In addition, staff have analyzed labs' safety practices, written about AI's effect on software engineers' speed, and studied the merits of using AI models to monitor other AI models. Barnes said she'd like to expand into predicting the next levels of AI's capabilities and how those changes could accelerate AI's development.

Neev Parikh, a METR researcher, says talent constraints limit the number of questions researchers can tackle about AI models' internal reasoning.

"There's a dearth of people," Parikh said. "I would happily see the field expand 10x."

METR could play a big role in a new AI climate

In July, OpenAI announced that its AI models cheated during testing by hacking into Hugging Face's systems to find the test answers. Later, CEO Sam Altman said it was "the first security incident that I have felt very viscerally."

METR had seen something like that coming. In May, the nonprofit wrote in a report that current AI agents "could plausibly start a rogue deployment," but would not have the skill to hide it. Then, in June, METR tried out OpenAI's then-unreleased GPT-5.6 Sol model and found that it would repeatedly cheat on challenging tests, including by extracting hidden source code to find the answers. It published a report about this and shared it with OpenAI before GPT-5.6 Sol's wider release.

Come July, the GPT-5.6 Sol model was part of OpenAI's security incident with Hugging Face. OpenAI announced on Wednesday that METR and another nonprofit, Redwood Research, would assess the incident and that their results would inform OpenAI's own technical report.

"There are now real, business-affecting incidents of this, and the world has a stake in understanding that," Painter said.

The cyber skills of OpenAI and Anthropic's newest models have sparked a wave of fear and attention and spawned a raft of new bills in Washington. METR's work lines up closely with one potential route for regulation: a current bill proposal would require large AI model developers to get safety audits from outside organizations. METR could fill a role like this; Painter said they'd potentially be interested, though it's something the field is still figuring out.

Something like that proposal, Painter said, could help with METR's hiring issue. He suggested that more people might leave the AI companies themselves — for similar salaries at METR, though without equity compensation — if a regulatory system gave safety research organizations greater authority.

"There's enough precedent here for each kind of testing arrangement," Painter said, "that I think with either clarity from industry, about how this testing should work long-term, or from the government, I think this field could scale very rapidly."

Ajeya Cotra, who led the writing of METR's May report on the risks of AI, said that oversight of AI can feel "chaotic and unpredictable" right now. She's still optimistic.

"The trend is toward people caring about this issue more," Cotra said. "And wanting to regulate it in a more serious way over time."

items.title: Reviews are ruining your life
items.summary: Getty Images; iStock; Tyler Le/BI James Hardaway has a reputation among his friends and family for being a reviews guy . Before making a big purchase, he'll check Wirecutter and Consumer Reports, do a drive-by of Reddit , and see what's being said on YouTube. He's an avid film fan, and he eagerly combs through Rotten Tomatoes scores and media writeups ahead of new releases to make sure he's in tune with the cultural moment. He feels that if he's not doing his homework, he may not be making the best use of his money. Still, Hardaway, a 38-year-old manufacturing manager in Texas, isn't sure if all the ratings-related rigamarole is meaningfully improving his life. He and his wife spent $450 on the supposed "best" stroller when their first child was born and swapped it out for cheaper options in a matter of months. He's not in love with their reviews-driven dishwasher or mattress, though he does like the internet-approved noise machine. For the most part, all the choices and all the noise leave him constantly wondering whether he could have done better. "There are more and more things that are getting reviewed," he says. "Maybe I don't need the best plunger, but something in my brain thinks that I do." Many Americans treat every product, service, and experience they buy like a research project. In 2016, the Pew Research Center found that eight in 10 Americans read online reviews before buying something for the first time, and more recent industry surveys suggest the habit has only become more entrenched. Case in point: a 2026 Yelp questionnaire found that an overwhelming majority of Gen Z consumers do research on at least one platform before picking a restaurant, gym, or beauty salon. Reviews are a remarkably useful invention that let us tap into the wisdom of the crowd. However, we may be taking review culture too far. We're drowning in endless options and endless opinions about those options. It leaves us less satisfied with our selections and strips spontaneity even from simple picks. Instead of helping us make good decisions quickly, reviews tempt us to believe there's some perfect decision to be found if we just keep scrolling. "Once you're out for the best, the path to misery is pretty straight," says Barry Schwartz, a professor emeritus in social theory and social action at Swarthmore College and the author of the book " The Paradox of Choice ." "It's the price we pay for getting what we said we wanted — which we shouldn't have wanted — which is unlimited options." Reviews have democratized information. Instead of relying on brand marketing or a newspaper critic (a dying breed anyway), people can learn from the experience of hundreds of other customers. But the volume of it all makes it easy to get overwhelmed. It's a familiar experience: You decide to have, say, pizza for dinner and start browsing through the local options. After 30 minutes, you've identified 15 possible restaurants and read dozens of reviews, and you are still no closer to a decision. One pizza is probably better than the other, but also, any pizza is probably fine, and here you are spending most of your Tuesday night on an unexpected, illogical quest to identify the ideal pie. Once you're out for the best, the path to misery is pretty straight. "One can get overly indexed on trying to find the best of something or all the information that they could find to make that perfect decision about it," says Michael Luca, a professor at Johns Hopkins Carey Business School. "When do we need to be optimizing? When do we need to be satisficing? And just finding something that works for what we're looking to do?" The internet reinforces the instinct. Google surfaces stars before websites, Amazon displays reviews before a price, and AI search engines increasingly summarize the online consensus before users see a link. Small businesses live and die by the algorithms and online rating systems. Having such an abundance of options can lead to anxiety and decision paralysis . Take the earlier dinner example: You may feel so inundated or dispirited that you forgo the pizza entirely and head to the kitchen to make a sandwich. Moreover, tastes vary, and we often don't know much, if anything, about the people whose perspectives we're using for guidance. "You're flipping coins because you don't know the source of any of these reviews, but somehow it gives your decision a certain authority that otherwise it wouldn't have," Schwartz says. The fact that our consumer choices are so intertwined with our identities gives each decision more weight, he adds: "The stakes go up for even trivial decisions, and that pushes even more in the direction of looking at what other people have to say and letting that guide your own decisions." As though the reviews themselves weren't enough, artificial intelligence is increasingly deciding which reviews people see and how they're interpreted, adding in a layer of complication for consumers and businesses alike. Some platforms are using AI to summarize reviews, boiling down hundreds of opinions into a handful of sentences. This may help consumers get a general sense of the feedback and make the reviews section feel more useful, but it also has its drawbacks. Power users who like to comb through ratings aren't going to get a lot out of a summary, and while research shows that AI summaries increase purchase intention for products like electronics and appliances, they don't move the needle for experiences, like restaurants and hotels. It's also not always clear whether an AI overview is accurate or surfaces the most pertinent information. It can flatten commentary into a generic package, overrepresent a small number of negative comments in an effort to be "fair," or simply get things wrong. On sites such as Reddit, it's easy to find small business owners lamenting that AI summaries include extra-negative or incorrect content. "AI could be helpful if it's helping to figure out how to tailor information and combine it to one's own preferences. But if it's doing more of a one-size-fits-all summary, it's not clear that it's getting you closer to that thing that specifically fits your preferences," Luca says. Doug Straton, the chief marketing officer at Bazaarvoice, a software company that helps brands collect and display ratings and reviews, says that when AI platforms crawl the web for reviews, they tend to look at volume, recency, and average rating. That is used to determine which products the bot talks about, but not necessarily what it says or the context opinions are coming from — maybe the reviewer the AI is channeling never likes the scent of cucumber, so they rate a bodywash negatively because of that, and all the AI reader sees is that it smells bad. "Because you're superficially scraping the sites, you don't have this depth of data," he says. Straton's company is working with AI companies to place more weight on the Bazaarvoice community's reviews, which they say are more trustworthy and thorough than the random ones. AI, of course, brings with it another issue: fakery . It's easier than ever to use AI tools to spin up reviews, and harder than ever for consumers to know what's AI-generated. To be sure, fake reviews are hardly new — Kay Dean, a former federal criminal investigator and the founder of Fake Review Watch, an industry watchdog, tells me they've long been a "massive" problem and that platforms aren't aggressive enough in cracking down on it. "They sweep it under the carpet," she says. You make a lot of choices, and most of them are irrelevant and unmemorable. There are all sorts of tactics, AI-related and otherwise, for engaging in review-related trickery, Dean says. Some businesses will barter and trade reviews, or even go to Facebook groups to enlist reviewers, while marketers may enlist review brokers. "There's a whole cottage industry of review providers," she says. "There is a robust black market, openly and flagrantly." The Federal Trade Commission has tried to crack down on fake reviews and, in 2024, put in place a rule that bans false ratings and testimonials, prohibits incentivizing reviews with a specific sentiment, and imposes financial penalties on violators. "It was a good step, but the review platforms escape liability," Dean says, because under federal law, online companies generally aren't liable for the content other people post on their platforms. We don't need to go back to a reviews-free society, where your best hope is that your neighbor has a decent recommendation for a contractor, but we probably could stand to adjust our approach when every single thing we might try or buy comes with a giant ratings system. Sheena Iyengar, a professor at Columbia Business School who studies choice and innovation, says it really helps for people to have clarity on their preferences and goals before diving into the online comments. If you're just looking for the "best" bar or the "best" gym, you're going to have a lot of work ahead of you and may very well end up disappointed. If, however, you're looking for a decent espresso martini at a relatively quiet place with lots of seating or an establishment with plenty of weights and spin classes, you're likely to be more satisfied with the results. We often flip through reviews faster than our brains can process the information, and in those cases, it's important to slow down, especially when it's a big decision, like booking a vacation . It's also key to remember that in the vast majority of situations, it's just not that deep. "You make a lot of choices, and most of them are irrelevant and unmemorable," Iyengar says. "Most of your choices in life, because of information overload, you probably should make them on autopilot, save your cognitive energy for the choices that matter." That's easier said than done for all the aforementioned reasons — the drive to find the best, the sense that every purchase says something about our identity. Yet there's something to be said for going with the flow. If the point of an evening is to catch up with a friend, there's no need to walk 20 blocks to what Yelp and TikTok say is the most happening spot instead of stopping at one of the eight places you pass on the way. Plus, you might discover at the end of your walk that a bunch of other optimization-seekers had the same idea, and now the place is too crowded to get in. Hardaway still checks reviews and probably always will. But he's learned the online chatter isn't the gospel and that no matter how much research he does, things may not work out. Sometimes, the best baby stroller isn't the one the gurus recommend — it's the one you actually wind up using. Emily Stewart is a senior correspondent at Business Insider, writing about business and the economy. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Third places are out, as prices rise. Hosting dinners, craft nights, and book clubs are in.
items.summary: Emily O'Brien and her friends have been meeting up for book club every month for roughly a year. Rachel Wisniewski for BI Emily O'Brien, 26, said in mid-July that she had about 200 pages to go in "Just for the Summer" by Abby Jimenez, before attending book club at a friend's place the following week. She loves attending the monthly meet-up, which friends take turns hosting at their homes in Philadelphia, a tradition they started roughly a year ago. She finished what she needed to read before gathering with her friends on a rooftop. Talking about the book is less important than making sure the friends meet every month to catch up without breaking the bank, she said. "It's paying off more so than just an occasional dinner would, in my opinion, because you're also sitting there and you just need to talk to one another," O'Brien said. O'Brien said people take turns hosting the book club. Rachel Wisniewski for BI She said that going out to dinner or happy hour every month can be expensive and hard to plan. "Do I really want to end up paying 80 bucks for a dinner and drinks with friends? Or I could just stay in and then not spend that," she said. "80 bucks now, I feel like, is different even than what 80 bucks was a year ago, where I'm like I need that for my groceries." Prices have skyrocketed since 2021, with food away from home rising about 32%, higher than food at home's 27% increase, based on the Bureau of Labor Statistics' consumer price index. The people who spoke to Business Insider find that hosting at home can mean more bang for their buck, since they're sharing food and drinks among many instead of a pricey meal for one or two at a night out, and have leftovers to enjoy. O'Brien is among the people in metros with a higher cost of living than the national average, bringing the " third place ," or the gathering space outside home and work, such as a coffee shop, into their "first place," or where someone lives. Whether for cost-related reasons or easier than gathering in public, people who spoke to Business Insider were looking to make a real effort to bring people together by hosting. "You either go to a third space to search out , or you can take responsibility and step up and volunteer to be the person in your community to make that happen," said Kristin Greene, who is in her 50s, and hosts a craft club on the third Tuesday of the month at her San Francisco home. Here's what some people are doing to intentionally foster community without going to a public space. Taking turns hosting a book club O'Brien hosted the book club twice, one of which she picked up brunch items from Trader Joe's , made floral arrangements, and set up a coffee bar with her Nespresso machine. She estimates she spent about $50 on the first session she hosted and about $75 on the other, but that's because she wanted to, and it doesn't have to be the case for everyone who wants to start bringing people together. O'Brien said people sometimes bring wine or an extra snack, yet the group has found it's best for the host to handle the rest, since everyone takes turns. She thinks it can be easy to avoid social situations because she lives alone, often visits her boyfriend, and wants to avoid the cost of going out. The book club keeps O'Brien accountable for staying connected with others, and although she likes to spend money when she hosts, she thinks it's worth it because it's an activity that brings her a lot of joy. O'Brien said the book club is more about connecting with friends than talking about the book itself. Rachel Wisniewski for BI Prices for food away from home, including dining out, and food at home, including groceries, have both grown about 36% from June 2019 to June 2026 in Philadelphia's metro area. Building a community at home in one of the most expensive metros Ariel and Cyrus Kashfian, who are in their 30s, have an open invitation for anyone who knows them or their plus ones to come to their Los Angeles apartment for Shabbat on Fridays. They also participate in other forms of hosting: Ariel is part of a monthly book club that rotates hosts, and the couple has hosted a murder mystery night with plans for another, among other gatherings. Cyrus said he likes bringing people together because he wouldn't otherwise see his friends. "If I don't make something happen, they aren't the ones to make plans and host and put things on the calendar," he said. He also thinks that going out to dinner continuously can get monotonous and feel less personal. "We could go out with friends and stuff like that, but it's harder to get close to people and to really spend quality time with them if you're not just together in someone's home or doing something in a very private environment," he said. Ariel, who said she and Cyrus are from family-oriented cultures, likes having people over and the positive effects it could have on their two children. "I want my kids to grow up with people always in and out and laughter and warmth," she said. "That's probably the most important part of growing up, is seeing people in your life that just show up for you and want to be around you and have fun." The children can also go to their rooms to play if they need a break from company, making it easier on the Kashfians than if they were taking care of their kids while out with friends. Plus, the couple lives in one of the most expensive metro areas in the US, based on regional price parities. "The price of going out in LA has become very, very, very high for a one-and-a-half-hour dinner," Ariel said. "You get more bang for your buck having people over at your house." Ariel said she made a pot roast, mashed potatoes, salads, and sides for their murder mystery night. While that added up pretty quickly in cost, she said they had leftovers, and everyone was happy with how the night turned out. "It was a memory that people will have for a very long time," she said. "Money and value are not also the same. You're getting a lot more for your dollar when you're hosting people, and doing an activity that's interesting and fun." items.title: Top economist Steve Hanke told us why he doubts AI will be the job destroyer many expect
items.summary: Steve Hanke says AI costs too much to be a major threat to jobs. Steve Hanke Steve Hanke says AI won't be the game changer many people imagine as it's "incredibly costly." The leading economist said the water, power, and microchips needed to power AI limit its potential. Hanke said that many companies won't replace people with AI because human labor will be cheaper. The idea that artificial intelligence will be free to use and virtually costless to provide is delusional and dumb, Steve Hanke says . "This belief is based on a disconnect from reality, as well as a good dose of idiotic economic reasoning," the professor of applied economics at Johns Hopkins University told Business Insider by email. "AI is incredibly costly; it is very resource intensive," Hanke continued. "It requires huge amounts of water, power, and physical capital" like graphics chips, he added. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta have projected roughly $700 billion in combined capital expenditures this year, and $1 trillion in 2027, as they race to build out the data centers needed to power the next generation of AI models. Hanke, who served on President Reagan's Council of Economic Advisers, also addressed widespread concerns that AI will cause massive job destruction . "Businesses will not be firing everybody and replacing them with AI ," he said, because in many cases that will be a lot more expensive than employing humans. The veteran economist took aim at AI visionaries, describing many of them as "charlatans and hucksters." He said they're "comparing apples and oranges" when they liken AI to software, as providing AI to customers costs money whereas software, once developed, can be sold countless times at virtually no additional cost. Hanke predicted the "cost of scarce resources that are gobbled up by AI will decide how far the 'AI revolution' goes." AI optimists have countered that technological advances will make microchips and data centers more power-efficient over time, bringing down the cost of AI. Elon Musk has made waves for predicting that AI will supercharge productivity and drive down production costs, ushering in an era of abundance where "anyone can have whatever stuff they want." The Tesla and SpaceX CEO has recommended people stop saving for retirement in 10 or 20 years as "money won't matter." Personal finance and AI experts previously told Business Insider they resoundingly disagreed with Musk's advice. Musk has predicted AI will take over most jobs, and the "best way" for governments to deal with the resulting unemployment is to provide a "universal high income" by mailing checks to everyone. Mounting concerns about AI Hanke has been skeptical of AI for a while, describing it to Business Insider in February as "overhyped and potentially dangerous." Last fall , Hanke said the AI boom could falter if Big Tech companies failed to hit their numbers, and said it "might be wise to buckle your seat belt." Mark Cuban, the former "Shark Tank" investor, and Michael Burry of "The Big Short" fame warned this week about the massive scale of AI spending and Nvidia's key role in financing it, underlining Hanke's concern about how much the technology costs. Cuban said it was "truly scary" how central Nvidia is to the AI boom, and cautioned it "all could crumble" if the chipmaker gets outcompeted or makes a mistake. Burry said Nvidia was "overreaching" in its campaign to strike deals with customers to support its chip sales, and its efforts threatened to "push the circular spending to biblical proportions." items.title: After Hugging Face incident, METR urges independent root-cause investigations into AI agent misbehavior
items.summary: Research organization METR is calling for systematic, independently led investigations whenever AI agents act autonomously against their developers' intentions. The push comes partly in response to the Hugging Face hack carried out by OpenAI models. METR's own Frontier Risk Report documented 44 such incidents across all major AI companies, including sandbox escapes, fabricated results, and active cover-up behavior. items.title: Snapchat Stops Recommending Fully AI-Generated Videos in Spotlight Feed
items.summary: Snap announced it will stop recommending "wholly AI-generated videos" in its Spotlight feed, prioritizing human-made content. This decision follows similar actions by YouTube , LinkedIn, and Substack in recent weeks to limit fully AI-generated material, often referred to as "AI slop." Snap will continue to allow AI-enhanced or edited videos in Spotlight recommendations. Snap stated on Friday that entirely AI-generated content is often low-quality, repetitive, and generally not aligned with user preferences. Snap Joins Other Platforms in Targeting AI Slop Snap’s update affects recommendations in the Spotlight feed but does not ban AI content entirely. The platform will no longer feature wholly AI-generated videos in Spotlight, instead highlighting authentic, human-made content. AI-enhanced or edited videos created with Snapchat’s tools will continue to be recommended. Snap acknowledged that fully AI-generated content is typically "low-quality," "repetitive," and not aligned with user interests. The Research supports these findings, and a separate survey indicates that increased exposure to AI-generated content reduces users’ trust in the authenticity of online material. Snap’s announcement follows similar measures implemented by other platforms in recent weeks. Substack introduced a tool to let readers detect AI-generated writing. Co-founder and CEO Chris Best said "it's getting harder to tell what's real on the internet" and cited research finding up to 40% of writing on social media is now fake or AI-generated. "Platforms that reward fakeness will create a race to the bottom," Best said. LinkedIn introduced a feature for users to report posts or comments that appear AI-generated. Chief Product Officer Hari Srinivasan reported the platform has "blocked billions" of AI-generated comment attempts and now intercepts hundreds of thousands daily. LinkedIn is also removing its AI-powered post enhancement prompt, reverting to a basic proofreading tool, and clarified that users who use AI to refine posts will not be affected by these measures. YouTube revised its monetization policies this month, specifying that generic, repetitive, or template-based content is ineligible for revenue. Research last year identified many YouTube channels comprised entirely of AI-generated content, some with millions of subscribers and significant revenue. YouTube’s trust and safety chief Matt Halprin stated that while AI technology "enables great stuff," it also facilitates content farming "that we don't want to have." What Snap’s Policy Change Means for AI Content The platforms share a consistent distinction: targeting fully AI-generated, low-effort content while permitting AI tools used to edit or refine human-made work. Snap, LinkedIn, and the others have each stated they are not rejecting AI use entirely, focusing instead on the automated, template-based content that generative tools make easy to produce at scale. Snap has not specified how it will distinguish wholly AI-generated videos from AI-enhanced content in Spotlight, or how this distinction will be enforced at scale. It is also unclear whether the change applies only to recommendations or to other areas of Snapchat, and Snap has not released data on the expected impact. The overall effectiveness of these measures against AI slop remains to be seen as implementation progresses. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. items.title: Square Enix Releases Final Fantasy 14 on Nintendo Switch 2 on August 4 With a Separate Subscription Requirement
items.summary: Square Enix has announced that Final Fantasy 14 will launch on Nintendo Switch 2 on August 4. The full MMORPG experience will be available, though performance will be lower than on more powerful platforms. The Switch 2 version requires a separate subscription and 117.2 GB of storage, but does not require a Nintendo Switch Online subscription. The port targets new players and provides existing users with a portable alternative. Final Fantasy 14 on Switch 2: Subscription and Storage Caveats Final Fantasy 14 on Switch 2 offers the same core MMORPG experience as other platforms, with extensive content. This release aims to make the game more accessible to a broader Nintendo audience. Performance on Switch 2 will be lower than on other platforms due to hardware limitations. The port also requires 117.2 GB of storage, which may be challenging for some users. Two factors may limit the port's appeal for current players. The Switch 2 version requires a separate subscription, so existing subscribers must pay again to play on this platform, which has disappointed some fans. However, a Nintendo Switch Online subscription is not required. The 117.2 GB file size is another concern, as it may exceed the Switch 2's internal storage. Both the subscription model and storage needs could limit adoption among existing players. Where Final Fantasy 14 on Switch 2 Fits in the Release Schedule The Switch 2 release is part of a broader Final Fantasy schedule. Final Fantasy Resonance, based on the Brave Exvius mobile game, arrives in October 2026. Final Fantasy 7 Revelation, the final entry in the FF7 remake trilogy, and the Evercold expansion for Final Fantasy 14 are both planned for 2027. items.summary_html:
Square Enix has announced that Final Fantasy 14 will launch on Nintendo Switch 2 on August 4. The full MMORPG experience will be available, though performance will be lower than on more powerful platforms.

The Switch 2 version requires a separate subscription and 117.2 GB of storage, but does not require a Nintendo Switch Online subscription. The port targets new players and provides existing users with a portable alternative.

Final Fantasy 14 on Switch 2: Subscription and Storage Caveats

Final Fantasy 14 on Switch 2 offers the same core MMORPG experience as other platforms, with extensive content. This release aims to make the game more accessible to a broader Nintendo audience.

Performance on Switch 2 will be lower than on other platforms due to hardware limitations. The port also requires 117.2 GB of storage, which may be challenging for some users.

Two factors may limit the port's appeal for current players. The Switch 2 version requires a separate subscription, so existing subscribers must pay again to play on this platform, which has disappointed some fans. However, a Nintendo Switch Online subscription is not required.

The 117.2 GB file size is another concern, as it may exceed the Switch 2's internal storage. Both the subscription model and storage needs could limit adoption among existing players.

Where Final Fantasy 14 on Switch 2 Fits in the Release Schedule

The Switch 2 release is part of a broader Final Fantasy schedule. Final Fantasy Resonance, based on the Brave Exvius mobile game, arrives in October 2026.

Final Fantasy 7 Revelation, the final entry in the FF7 remake trilogy, and the Evercold expansion for Final Fantasy 14 are both planned for 2027.

Players interested in the Switch 2 version should consider the following points:

  1. A separate subscription is required; existing Final Fantasy 14 subscriptions on other platforms do not transfer to Switch 2.
  2. At least 117.2 GB of storage is needed, which may require a microSD Express card due to limited internal capacity.
  3. Performance will be lower than on PC, PlayStation, or Xbox because of the Switch 2's hardware limitations.
  4. A Nintendo Switch Online subscription is not required, which helps offset some of the additional subscription cost.
Availability

Final Fantasy 14 launches on Nintendo Switch 2 on August 4. Square Enix has not yet explained how character or progress sharing will work between Switch 2 and other platforms, nor has it confirmed the exact pricing for the separate subscription.

The port's success will depend on both existing players seeking portability and newcomers, with the Evercold expansion set for 2027.
